- [ ] **GEN.534 A satellite's young stars reach the system-type tables: the young-star system types name `satellite_young`**
  Residual of GEN.528 (merged #2077, 2026-10-17, about 3:02 PM EDT as
  Core 3 reported), filed by the TODO thread from Core 3's report.
  GEN.528 built the satellite's gas, remnants, magnetars and planetary
  nebulae, but not the young stars in the system-type tables:
  `satellite_young` is in `system_types.POPULATIONS`, yet no system-type
  row names it and the young-star types list only the disk's young
  population (finding from GEN.526, Core 3, 12:16 PM EDT). Core 3 left
  it because nothing in `system_types` keys on `satellite_young` today.
  Do: let the young-star system types (the types that need a young
  population) draw from `satellite_young` in a Magellanic cell, with the
  weight derived from the satellite's young share, not set by hand.
  Done: a system asked inside the Large Cloud can be a young-star type,
  a system in a dwarf with no young stars cannot, a test shows both, and
  the epoch rule applies (a stored-value change joins the pending epoch
  and the one rescatter). Owner: Core 3 (proposed, GEN.528's author;
  behind its queue).
  Prerequisites: none. Related: GEN.528, GEN.526, GEN.319.

- [ ] **GEN.535 Check the Magellanic gas fraction and supernova-remnant count against the observed Clouds, and the dwarfs that still come out with gas (Leo I)**
  Open inferences of GEN.528 (merged #2077, 2026-10-17, about 3:02 PM
  EDT as Core 3 reported), filed by the TODO thread from Core 3's
  report. (1) The gas fraction of a satellite is the young stars'
  density against the solar circle's through the Schmidt-Kennicutt
  exponent (0.33 at the Large Cloud's centre, 0.89 at the Small
  Cloud's), an inference and not a measured gas map. (2) The Large Cloud
  keeps about 7 of 67 remnant candidates, so its count is low against
  the real Cloud's roughly 60 remnants. (3) Leo I still comes out with
  gas, because its recalled mean age is from GEN.369. Do: read the
  observed gas masses or fractions of the two Clouds and of Leo I
  (verified sources only, citations checked first), compare them with
  the generated fractions, and find why the remnant count is low (the
  kept fraction, the age range of the remnant progenitors or the gas
  fraction at the radius); fix the derivation if a law explains it, else
  record the gap in the gap plan with a label. Done: the generated gas
  fraction and remnant count of each Cloud sit within the observed range
  (or the gap is labelled and tunable), Leo I's gas follows a verified
  age, and the research is dated on the goal issue. Owner: unowned
  (research, then Core 3 for the fix).
  Prerequisites: none. Related: GEN.528, GEN.369, GEN.526.

- [ ] **GEN.536 Research the velocity dispersion of molecular gas (CO) in nearby spirals to set the young stars' scale height**
  Filed by the TODO thread from Core 1's GEN.532 report (2026-10-17,
  3:12 PM EDT as the lane reported). The generator's gas dispersion is
  10 +/- 2 km/s (Tamburro 2009), which is the atomic (HI) value, so the
  young stars' scale height comes out 0.40 of the old disc's (116 pc for
  a 300 pc disc) against the observed about 50 pc; molecular gas is
  colder and its dispersion was not read. Do: find a measured CO
  velocity dispersion in a sample of nearby spirals (verified sources
  only, citations checked first, read in full or marked as not read),
  give the value and scatter against galaxy mass or Vc where the data
  allow, and say what the young scale height becomes. Done: the research
  is dated on the goal issue and labelled READ or NOT REACHED, the value
  and its source are recorded for the stand-in registry, and the
  replacement of the 10 km/s young-population dispersion is its own item
  if the law is found. Owner: unowned (research; Boss or a read-only
  research lane). This is a Boss research item.
  Stand-in in GEN.532 (Core 1, 2026-10-17, 5:55 PM EDT as the lane
  reported): the first gate of GEN.532 showed the atomic-gas 10 km/s
  made the young disc 0.40 of the old disc's height (nebula counts over
  the ceiling: class M 22,804 against 20,000), so GEN.532 carries a
  molecular birth-gas stand-in of 6.5 +/- 1 km/s (young disc 0.22 of the
  old), labelled as replaced by this item. The reading to compare the
  research against is the old atomic one (10 km/s, 0.40) and the
  observed about 50 pc; the stand-in value itself has no source and is
  entered in the stand-in registry as a placeholder.
  Prerequisites: none. Related: GEN.532, GEN.531.

- [ ] **GEN.537 Design the plan configuration: the boundaries of the sector plan, how far scatters go, which sector addresses are valid, and the two switches halo and satellite galaxies (both default off)**
  Boss, 2026-10-17, 4:31 PM EDT: "begin planning for the halo and
  intergalactic generation to be a switch that defaults to off, put that
  in for 8.5 please, we'll get it working first." Changed by Boss,
  2026-10-17, 4:48 PM EDT: "Make there be 2 switches, halo and satellite
  galaxies, both default to off, halo doesn't mean satellite galaxies,
  they are separate commands used to configure the plan. That plan
  configuration tells scatter and sector generation the boundaries of
  the sector plan and control how far scatters can go around the galaxy
  and what sector addresses are valid." What exists (read from main,
  2026-10-17): the plan's boundaries are `GalaxyBounds`
  (galaxy/skeleton.py): the reach (`reach_shell_index`, set by `plan
  --reach-shells`, stored in `galaxy_shape` with the outline in
  `galaxy_shell`), whose `contains` says which sector addresses are
  valid and is today the only refusal a generation path has (GEN.235),
  and the outline, whose `qualifies` is where the paths that pick cells
  nobody named stay; how far a scatter goes is not in the plan but the
  program constant `tuning.SCATTER_COVERS_REACH = True`, read in
  generation/run_plan.py (the bright-star and phenomena scatters);
  satellite galaxies are placed unconditionally by
  `satellites.place_satellites` inside the plan build (run_plan.py,
  `generation/satellites.py`). Version 8.1 builds the halo and the
  satellite galaxies first, always on (GEN.301). Done: a design note
  (docs/design) that settles, with Boss by card: (1) the plan
  configuration as the single source of the boundaries of the sector
  plan, how far each scatter can go around the galaxy, and which sector
  addresses are valid, read by the scatter commands and by sector
  generation, which never decide those themselves (it replaces the
  `SCATTER_COVERS_REACH` constant and the reach and outline checks
  scattered through generation, and extends `GalaxyBounds`, which
  already holds the reach and the outline); (2) two switches, halo and
  satellite galaxies, both default off and independent (halo does not
  mean satellite galaxies): what each adds to the valid addresses and to
  the scatter reach (halo: the cells beyond the outline out to the reach
  and the scatter rows there; satellite galaxies: the volumes of the
  satellite galaxies and their stars, which may lie beyond the outline),
  and what off means (nothing generated or stored there, the interior
  the same stars for the same seed whether either is on or off, an
  address outside the configured boundaries answers "outside the
  generated galaxy" with the reason); (3) each switch is set by its own
  command under the one-command rule (PERF.118, PERF.120): a halo
  command and a satellite-galaxies command, each doing only that and
  writing only the plan configuration, with their own parameters; the
  262 kpc reach and the 96-bit IDs stay as addressing; (4) where the
  configuration is stored (proposed: beside the galaxy shape, set by a
  migration from what an existing galaxy holds, so a galaxy built in 8.1
  with both on keeps them on, and default off for a galaxy created after
  8.5); (5) what turning a switch on later does (the missing part only,
  no interior regeneration) and what turning it off does (generation
  stops and the maps hide it; deleting what exists is the separate admin
  delete); (6) how the wrapper uses it: the step list holds the halo and
  satellite commands only when the configuration allows them, so a
  switch that is off means those commands are never selected and never
  touched. Owner: the design thread (coordinator to assign); Boss
  approves the choices by card.
  Prerequisites: none. Related: GEN.301, PERF.118, PERF.121, GEN.235,
  MAP.243, MAP.207.
  Added (Boss, 2026-10-17, 4:49 PM EDT: "the galaxy setting will also
  tell the scatter functions if they can scatter the halo and / or the
  satellite galaxies, either / or"): the stored galaxy setting (halo on
  or off, satellite galaxies on or off) is read by every scatter
  command, and each scatter kind checks only the switch that concerns
  it: the halo scatter kinds read the halo switch, the satellite and
  satellite-component scatter kinds read the satellite switch, the kinds
  that concern neither (the disc, bulge and core scatters) read neither;
  either switch can be on without the other. The design settles which
  scatter kind reads which switch.
  Decided (Boss, 2026-10-17, card tapped 4:56 PM EDT, "Migrate in 8.5",
  relayed by the coordinator): a galaxy created in 8.1 keeps its halo
  and satellite content, and the 8.5 migration sets that galaxy's halo
  and satellite galaxy switches to on if it holds that content (each
  switch on its own); only a galaxy created after 8.5 defaults both off.
  No change to 8.1. Point (4) of this design is therefore settled.

  2020 (abstract level for the last three). The failed-supernova share
  of stars of 8 to 150 Msun is 0 to 45% (solar metallicity: 0 to 7%
  O'Connor and Ott, 5 to 21% Ebinger, 26 to 45% Sukhbold; low
  metallicity 15 to 32%; observations allow 0 to about 0.4), more at low
  metallicity, so the black hole share of stars born is 0 to 0.29% and
  the density 0 to 4.0e-4 per pc^3; no single central value exists. The
  present 7e-5 per pc^3 (0.05%) equals f = 7.8%: inside the verified
  range, near its low end. Remnant: birth baryonic mass 2.1 to 2.5 Msun,
  then 7.7 to 9.2 Msun (helium core) or 13.2 to 13.8 Msun (whole star)
  on average (Sukhbold); gravitational mass 0.9 of baryonic (Fryer). The
  0.17% in the design thread's quick check counted every progenitor of
  20 to 100 Msun, not a failed-supernova share. Still not verified: the
  kick-escape share, Zhang 2008, Smartt 2009, Kochanek 2015, Ugliano
  2012. This item stays open for the moons, isolated-disk and size-law
  parts.
  Contradiction sweep (Boss's request, 2026-10-18, 5:44 PM EDT; the
  newer note wins, report todo-contradictions-2026-10-18.md): O'Connor
  and Ott 2011, Sukhbold et al. 2016 and Fryer et al. 2012 are verified
  (finding of 2026-10-17, 11:55 PM EDT); the Do list's "recalled and
  unverified" no longer applies to them. The kick-escape share stays
  unverified.
  Prerequisites: none. Related: GEN.550.

- [ ] **GEN.564 A refill job for a galaxy under an older generator epoch: clear the fill-level rows of every sector and rebuild them without a rescatter**
  Filed proposed, not assigned, from Core 1's read-only code audit of
  main at 5c49fc42 (11:50 PM EDT as the lane reported; a helper read it,
  Core 1 did not re-verify each line, no code was run), answering the
  back-scatter question whether a refill is enough for the fill-level
  8.4 changes (unified chain GEN.553 to GEN.559, the composition chain,
  DB.73 and DB.67 to DB.71). Result: yes for stars, systems, planets,
  moons, belts and comets; not yet for scattered phenomena. What exists:
  `POST /api/sectors/<id>/regenerate` (`api/edits.py`, job
  `regenerate_sector`, `queue/api_jobs.py` about 270 to 300) calls
  `delete_sector_with_contents` (`db/edits.py` 346 to 375) then
  `run_galaxy.ensure_sector_generated`; it deletes a sector's star
  systems (planets, moons, stars, belts and comets by cascade) and its
  stand-alone phenomenon rows (black holes, neutron stars, nebulae,
  supernova remnants, rogue planets, interstellar comets, asteroid
  fields, quasars), facilities and nearest systems, and keeps
  `phenomenon_scatter`, `scatter_members`, `scatter_nodes`,
  `nebula_field` and `bright_stars` (foreign key ON DELETE SET NULL, so
  they become unbuilt and rebuild). Gaps a bulk job must close: (A) the
  delete does not reset `phenomenon_scatter.built_at` or
  `phenomenon_scatter_classes.built` (only `mark_phenomena_built` writes
  `built_at`, `store.py` 6212 to 6223, and the fill reads `built_at IS
  NULL`, 6204 to 6209), so scattered black holes, neutron stars,
  remnants, planetary nebulae, hypervelocity stars and the nucleus would
  vanish and not come back: the job resets them for the cell (a write to
  a scatter table, no redraw); (B) systems built from one bright star
  with no sector (`generate_uncharted_system_job`, `api/routes.py` 1245
  to 1272) are missed by a sector-keyed clear: select them through
  `bright_stars.star_system_id`; (C) `species.homeworld_planet_id` and
  facilities cascade, so the population and sector paths rerun; (D)
  object UIDs are issued in insertion order (`store.py` 7737 and after)
  and are public in URLs, so if 8.4 changes how many planets or moons a
  system gets, body UIDs shift: a decision for Boss and the identity
  chain (it bears on 'a planet that leaves its star keeps its ID'); (E)
  the generator epoch is never compared at runtime
  (`util/generator_epoch.py` feeds the estimate cache key and the
  bump_version check only, no database column stores it; each sector
  records `version_key` and `planetgen_version`), so a job needs a way
  to tell which sectors are old. Findings on dependence: the fill copies
  scatter values in and links back, so a changed fill draw breaks no
  link; nothing in `generation/` or `db/store.py` reads
  `scatter_members`, `scatter_nodes` or `member_count` today, and the
  planned 'fill builds from stored members' (GEN.264, GEN.315, 8.1)
  would make a clear lose the stored trees, so a refill after GEN.315
  must keep or rebuild them. Do: a bulk job (CLI and queue command)
  that, for every sector or a chosen range, clears the fill-level rows,
  resets the phenomena built flags, handles the sector-less uncharted
  systems, reruns population, and rebuilds; it refuses when a sector's
  version marks it current. Done: after an epoch bump that changes only
  fill output, the job brings a test galaxy to the same rows as a fresh
  fill of the same seed, without touching a scatter row, and says what
  it did per sector. Owner: Core 1 (proposed; it owns the identity and
  repair chain and the regenerate path), 8.4 phase 1.
  Boss tapped 'IDs stay stable' (11:49 PM EDT, 2026-10-17, as the
  coordinator relayed): gap (D) is closed by DB.75, a prerequisite of
  this item: a refill must not renumber the bodies of a system whose
  planet or moon count changes, and a body that changes parent keeps its
  ID.
  Decided (Boss, contradiction sweep cards, taps 6:08 to 6:10 PM EDT
  2026-10-18, as the coordinator reported them): fork 2, "Epoch bump
  plus refill": fill-level 8.4 items (stars, systems, planets, moons,
  belts, comets, rogue planets, free brown dwarfs) take the epoch bump
  and the GEN.564 refill, not a rescatter; the one wiped rescatter stays
  in 8.1, and only scatter-level changes (nebula radius, remnants above
  the mass cut) need a rescatter. Where this item says it "joins the one
  rescatter of 8.4", this wins.
  Prerequisites: DB.75. Related: GEN.550, GEN.315, DB.73.

- [ ] **GEN.565 The mass object core and its three family classes: StellarObject, PlanetaryObject and SmallBody, with state and parent as data, replace the nine kind classes**
  Part of the unified orbited-body chain (GEN.550; design note
  docs/design/mass-object-class.md, decided: Boss's cards, as the
  coordinator relayed with the wake times converted: E2 tapped
  'Representability floor' at 11:46 PM EDT; E1 typed 'ok, I approve in
  the hybrid approach you outlined, let it to TODO and ship to into the
  plan' in the unified star-like objects thread at 11:48 PM EDT; E3
  tapped 'Inside host chain' at 11:48 PM EDT; E4 tapped 'Plan only' at
  11:49 PM EDT; the object-ID card 'IDs stay stable' at 11:49 PM EDT
  (2026-10-17)). Owners follow Boss's card D7 (Core 4 chain and classes,
  Core 1 storage). U4a of the design. Do: a `MassObject` core holding
  what every body has (identity and ID, name, mass, radius, state vector
  relative to its parent with `parent_type` and `parent_id`, age, spin,
  galactic motion, sector and place, timestamps, serialization from one
  field table), and three family classes under it where behaviour lives:
  `StellarObject` (`Star`, `CompactRemnant`, `BlackHole`, `NeutronStar`
  and the brown dwarf fold into it as states: protostar,
  pre-main-sequence, main sequence, giant, white dwarf, neutron star,
  black hole, brown dwarf; the `_skip_property_init` workaround goes),
  `PlanetaryObject` (`Planet` with its `is_moon`, `RoguePlanet`: a moon is a planetary object whose parent is a
  planet, a rogue planet one with no parent), `SmallBody` (`Comet`,
  `InterstellarComet`, belt and field members). Rule: subclass only
  where behaviour differs and the object never changes kind; anything
  that can change or is a matter of degree is state or parent data.
  Groups (the nodes of a multi-star tree) are not bodies and stay
  `OrbitNode`. The floor (E2): the class can represent any body of 10 m
  diameter (5 m radius) or more across about 34 orders of magnitude of
  mass (1.05e6 kg for a 10 m rock to the 2.0e40 kg black hole), with
  every position relative to the parent, never galaxy-absolute (10 m at
  262 kpc is a relative precision of 1e-21, beyond a double); rows are
  generated from each population's own cut (a planet or moon always, a
  comet above its size cut, belt members on demand: the k-th largest
  member of a belt is a pure function of the belt's seed and k, nothing
  stored). E4: the core is planned to take ships and stations
  (`facilities` has no mass or size column) in 9.3, and nothing is built
  for them now. E3: built inside the host chain, not as a separate
  refactor; it removes the 17 copies of five rules (the white dwarf
  initial-final relation in four places, the NS/BH mass in five, three
  age rules, two Schwarzschild formulas, two Burrows luminosities) with
  GEN.553, and the serializers and constructor boilerplate of the nine
  classes (about 300 to 360 and 170 to 350 lines; whole net saving about
  800 to 1,800 of about 9,000 lines touched, the design thread's own
  estimate and not measured by running anything). Risk to watch: the
  orbital update steps planets and moons as state vectors, stars and
  wanderers by galactic-orbit phase, comets by their own Kepler state,
  and the nightly batch order is the easiest place to break
  reproducibility; one state vector for all is a real saving that was
  not measured. Done: the nine classes are gone with no shim, every kind
  loads and stores through the core and its profile, and the golden
  output is unchanged by the refactor itself (it bumps no epoch unless
  folded into GEN.553's changes). Owner: Core 4 (Boss's card D7, 11:28
  to 11:31 PM EDT as relayed), built with GEN.553 and GEN.557; 8.4 phase
  1.
  Prerequisites: none. Related: GEN.550, GEN.553, GEN.557, GEN.556,
  GEN.552.
  Units (Boss's cards Q1 to Q6, 11:56 to 11:57 PM EDT, as the

  chain: collect the members with their original values, rank them by
  total branch mass (a sub-system counts as the sum of its parts; a tie
  under 1e-9 relative keeps the draw order, so the step is stable and
  idempotent and does not depend on the order members are listed), nest
  by distance (members inside the demoted body's stable zone stay with
  it as a sub-system, members outside the pair's orbit orbit the pair's
  barycentre, members in the unstable gap are moved or dropped by the
  existing outermost-first rule), recompute everything that depends on
  the primary from the original values, then validate. Two bodies:
  re-primarying a pair is a relabel plus a sign (the relative position
  is negated, the phase moves by 180 degrees, the elements and the
  barycentre are unchanged) and every absolute position is identical.

  `generation/wide_binary.py:119-121` and `generation/binary.py`
  (GEN.316 already retires the two-star classes). GEN.555 and GEN.556
  need it. Done: a pair re-primaried gives identical absolute positions,
  the step from the originals is idempotent and independent of listing
  order, and no second copy of the swap is left.

  rate. Add named unit systems, each a list of base units (SI; AU, year

  answered). About 15 relations cover the hand-written laws

  `galactic_orbit(position, velocity)` (GEN.584 reads them for the
  derived columns). The dimension test runs each formula once on probe
  objects that carry a dimension and checks the result has the declared
  output dimension, in the `physics/mathcheck.py` invariant group
  (TEST.65); a km where m was meant or a missing square fails the gate,
  nothing is checked at run time. About 250 to 350 lines with tests.
  Done: each relation has a kernel, a wrapper and a dimension test; a
  deliberately wrong formula fails the gate; kernel and wrapper agree
  bit for bit on the golden inputs; the module header states the unit
  rules and that kernels take plain SI floats.

  GEN.569.

- [ ] **GEN.589 Research: the central molecular zone's upper cluster mass and its cloud-shock disruption, so the young clusters of the core match the few that are observed**
  Finding from Core 3 while building GEN.244 and GEN.282 (1:58 AM EDT
  2026-10-18 as the lane reported), filed by the TODO thread. Kind:
  generation result against observation. Object: the central molecular
  zone ring of a drawn galaxy. Result: 5 to 12 young clusters above 5e3
  solar masses per galaxy against about 2 observed (Arches and
  Quintuplet), and 7 to 21 clusters older than 10 Myr above 5e4 against
  none. Cause as the lane reads it: the cluster mass function M^-2 runs
  to 1e6 solar masses (the widest limit under Boss's widest-range rule),
  the ambient density of the disruption law leaves out the gas, and
  there is no disruption by cloud shocks. Do (research first, nothing
  built until the sources are read): find a published upper cluster mass
  for the central molecular zone and a cloud-shock disruption rate (Core
  3 names Trujillo-Gomez 2019 as a lead; it is a lead until a lane has
  read it, and a lane verifies each citation before use), say what the
  sources give, and propose the change to GEN.244's mass function and
  disruption for the core ring; the fill ships as the labelled stand-in
  meanwhile. A change to the stored clusters rides the pending epoch and
  the one wiped rescatter. Done: the note names the sources with their
  evidence state, gives the upper mass and the disruption law with their
  scatter, and a test shows the young clusters of the core above 5e3
  solar masses are few (the observed count is the plausibility target,
  not a preset). Owner: Core 3 (proposed; it built GEN.244). Not a
  prerequisite of GEN.301.
  Prerequisites: none. Related: GEN.244, GEN.282.

- [ ] **GEN.599 A run with missing downloaded data files refuses unless it is told explicitly to disregard them, and then uses the best possible fallback and says so in its header**
  Boss, 2026-10-21, 5:54 PM EDT, as the coordinator relayed: "Also
  revision of my previous choice, have the best possible fallback if the

  to disregard missing files. Also-also, the updater / downloader should
  list the file URL it's loading as well." This replaces the 'Require
  the data' rule (Boss, 9:38 AM EDT 2026-10-18, GEN.590) and the
  refuse-or-fall-back cards of GEN.594. Today
  `run_galaxy.require_datasets` refuses a bulk run while any catalogue
  file is missing, and `fetch.DataMissing` is raised by readers, so no
  value ever comes from a fallback (src/planetgen/datasets/fetch.py,
  stellar_abundances.py). Do: keep the refusal as the default, with a
  plain message naming each missing file, its URL and the setup command
  (`python3 -m planetgen.cli.datasets fetch KEY`); add one explicit
  option that tells the run to disregard missing files (proposed:
  `--disregard-missing-data` on the CLI commands and `update.sh` runs,
  and a labelled checkbox on the Generate page and a field on the API
  job, off by default; the owner may pick the exact words); with it set,
  every reader of a missing dataset takes its best possible fallback
  (the labelled stand-in of the gap registry, section 6.6, or for star
  composition the best available relation), never silently: the run

  missing file and no option refuses with the file names and URLs; with

  Blocker 2 proposed (it picks the work up after or between its seven

- [ ] **GEN.603 Shape dials: the Scale dial: mass override, compactness in sigma, density, and the any-two-of-three pin logic with the third shown**
  Boss (galaxy size research thread, 2026-10-21): 6:41 PM EDT chose
  mass, size and density as one 'any two of three' group with the third

  /mnt/project-files/reports/galaxy-size-2026-10-21.md. Resolution
  order: the seed draws mass and the compactness z; a pinned lever
  replaces its draw; then mass, then size (from compactness, an absolute

  names which was dropped. A dial replaces only its draw's median; the
  draw's random number is untouched, so the same seed at a new mass
  gives the same residuals in sigma (turning the dial moves the galaxy
  smoothly). Mass range widens to the size law's source span (GEN.609).
  Done: tests for each pair of pins reproducing the third within
  tolerance; the refusal and its message; same seed, mass doubled, gives
  the same size sigma and thick disc sigma; no pin gives today's galaxy
  exactly.

  never keeps a cache. Decided (Boss, 2026-10-10 18:44Z, defaults
  approved; default): decide after
  PERF.31 shows the cold rebuild cost; switch if a full rebuild takes
  more than a minute.

  Done: a note (docs/design/gravity-map.md, section 'How it is
  computed', extended with measurements) says what a grid of 16 zones
  per edge costs for a dense sector (core, bulge and arm) and a sparse
  one, with numpy and the per-region aggregates of MAP.151, picks the
  near/far distance and the zone count, gives the error of the aggregate
  against the exact sum, and says when a grid is recomputed after an

  the near and far distance and the zone count, state the error); no
  kernel code of its own.

  subtask and all of that. It's going to be a lot of work too but I
  think I'm wasting a lot of efficiency." Done: a design note on what

- [ ] **PERF.111 `ResponseCache.put` without a database never trims the page cache: the cache grows past `max_entries`, and the thread test fails when its last put is one of those (bug)**
  Found by Core 2 (2026-10-17, 6:31 AM EDT as the lane reported, MAP.217
  gate unit phase), filed by the TODO thread, who read the code.
  `src/planetgen/web/lib/pagecache.py` `ResponseCache.put`: the `db is
  None` branch stores the entry and returns without the `while
  len(self._entries) > self._max_entries: popitem()` that the keyed
  branch (and `_recall`) have, so entries of the no-database kind are
  never evicted. Test:
  `src/tests/test_caches_threads.py::test_page_cache_fills_reads_and_clears_from_many_threads`
  failed with `assert 51 <= 50`. Fails on main: yes (deterministic).
  Frequency: 1 of 1 in the MAP.217 gate unit phase (1 failed, 18,311
  passed, 3,793 s); it passes alone 3 of 3 because it fails only when
  the last put of the run is a db=None one. Reproducer, no threads:
  `cache = pagecache.ResponseCache(lambda db, since: {"stamp": "s",
  "state": None}, dict(pagecache.DEFAULTS, max_entries=3,
  stamp_seconds=0))`, then 6 times `cache.put(None, f"/x/{n}", "body",
  cache.begin(None))`: `len(cache)` is 6, should be 3. Do: the same trim
  loop in the db-None branch (inside the lock, after the store), and a
  deterministic test of the reproducer above next to the thread test.
  Done: the reproducer gives 3, the thread test passes whatever the last
  put is, and a test asserts the bound for db=None puts alone. Owner:
  Core 2 (proposed; it offered to carry the three lines in its next PR,
  which is the cheapest route).
  Checked by the TODO thread (2026-10-17, 6:28 AM EDT, main with #2004):
  the reproducer above gives len(cache) 6 with max_entries 3, so the
  finding stands.
  Owner: Bug Hunt (bugs only, Boss, 2026-10-17, 10:06 AM EDT). This
  replaces any earlier owner line on this item.
  Prerequisites: none. Related: PERF.104, TEST.54.

- [ ] **PERF.113 The neighbour link of a galaxy run: measure it, and split it into chunks of sectors if the time warrants**
  Boss, 2026-10-17, 4:06 PM EDT: all generation tasks should be
  parallelized in a way that helps (a thread per chunk for scatters, a
  worker per sector for sector generation). Audit finding: `link`
  (`store.link_sector_neighbors`, db/store.py, called by the `galaxy`
  command) runs on one connection in one process in batches of
  LINK_BATCH_SECTORS, and PERF.107 only moves it onto the queue as ONE
  one-shot unit. Done: the stage is timed and the figure recorded; if it
  justifies it, `link` becomes static chunks of sectors (each chunk
  writes only its own sectors' neighbour rows, so chunks cannot
  collide), with the run-record barrier before `population`. Same rule
  for every stage: measure first. Time the stage on an idle box for a
  galaxy of the size a real run makes and write the figure in the PR;
  split it into parallel units only if that time is large enough to
  matter (about a minute or more), otherwise leave it as one unit and
  say so in the PR. Either way the result must be identical for the same
  seed at 1 and at 4 workers (a test that compares the stored rows), and
  the units are static chunks, not a work-stealing split, so a rerun
  gives the same chunks.
  Prerequisites: none. Related: PERF.98, PERF.107.

  to matter (about a minute or more), otherwise leave it as one unit and

  seed at 1 and at 4 workers (a test that compares the stored rows), and
  the units are static chunks, not a work-stealing split, so a rerun
  gives the same chunks.

- [ ] **PERF.119 The Generate page, the API and the one-off sector and system commands start their runs through the wrapper**
  Boss, 2026-10-17, 4:12 PM EDT: "Rework so every part of the generate
  process, all the scatter phases, are individual commands, then a
  general process wrapper makes a list of the commands that need to be
  run, and then puts those into the redis queue individually." The
  wrapper builds the command list, each command is one queue item. Once
  the stages are commands (PERF.106 to PERF.108), every way to start
  generation uses the one wrapper of PERF.118: the Generate page
  (`web/generate_page.py`, `web/job_runner.py`), the API jobs
  (`queue/api_jobs.py`) and the one-off `planetgen sector` and
  `planetgen system` commands (each a one-command run), so there is no
  second way to run a stage and no start path that skips the run record.
  Done: each of those entry points builds its command list with the
  wrapper and queues it; a test starts a run from each and finds it on
  the run record; a grep finds no stage started outside the wrapper.
  Owner: Core 5 (after PERF.98, before PERF.99 reads the run record on
  the pages).
  Decided (Boss, 2026-10-17, 4:15 PM EDT): from the command line Boss
  runs `plan`, then `scatter`; each scatter kind is its own command even
  where the root command is the same (a scatter command for only mass,
  only luminosity, only phenomena, only the nebula field, only the
  backfill, and so on, never one command that groups them). Each command
  has its own parameters, which the UX sets when it runs the commands
  through the API and which Boss sets on the command line. When a new
  generate job is called, the wrapper ONLY selects the commands that
  will run and never touches the others; they run in sequence; the
  progress bars are dynamic to the current context and show only what is
  going to run (the overall bar, the stage count and the estimate come
  from the selected commands alone). So each entry point sends its own
  parameters per command, and its progress shows only the commands
  selected.
  Decided (Boss, 2026-10-17, 4:18 PM EDT): the governing principle of
  PERF.118 holds for every start path: each entry point only builds the
  list of steps from what the user requested and hands it to the
  wrapper, which alone handles the sequence.
  The command inventory (docs/design/command-inventory.md, PERF.120)
  lists every other command and entry point.
  Decided (Boss, 2026-10-18, 5:14 to 5:15 PM EDT, cards F1 to F4, all as
  Core 5 recommended, relayed by the coordinator): F1 'One wrapper run':
  the Generate page builds the command list and one wrapper run follows
  it, and `web/job_runner.py` only starts that run detached (it does not
  build or order commands). F2: reset, check-math and the like are
  one-unit registry commands. F3: each API job is a small run of its own.
  F4: `planetgen sector` and `planetgen system` go through the wrapper
  (each a one-command run).
  Prerequisites: PERF.98. Related: PERF.99, PERF.118.

- [ ] **PERF.129 Robust tile caching: the first zoom levels built ahead, tiles stored compressed, built proactively around every visit, kept until the data changes**
  Boss, 2026-10-17, 4:31 PM EDT: "for 8.2 I want to add robust tile
  caching, so that we build out not only the initial galactic view but
  all the normal zoom levels for that view that we can compress and
  serve up to the client immediately on request. Basically I want to
  build out tiles for the first several zoom levels and then I want to
  build it so that system is proactive and when the user visits and zoom
  level it builds and caches all the surrounding tiles and the next zoom
  levels. Then it keeps them until the data changes." What exists (read
  from main, 2026-10-17): `web/lib/tilecache.py` keeps packed tiles on
  disk (`<cache dir>/<db>/<generation>/<tile>.bin`, the PGT1 format of
  `tilepack.py`), answers `/galaxy/tiles` by joining stored bytes, and
  keeps stage and window payloads the same way; freshness is the content
  stamp plus `GET /api/galaxy/changes` (the `modified_at` columns, so
  only the changed tiles are deleted, and a change that cannot be pinned
  to tiles starts a new generation); `prune` deletes the least recently
  written files above `tile_cache.max_mb`; the browser keeps its own
  copy in IndexedDB (MAP.158); `web/warmup.py` warms only the opening
  view's tiles and the galaxy stage; Apache compresses each response at
  send time; the admin health block shows where the cache lives and its
  size. Goal (done when its subitems are): the Galaxy Map answers any
  tile of the first several zoom levels at once from a stored compressed
  copy; a visit to any zoom level builds and caches the surrounding
  tiles and the next level's tiles before they are asked for; every
  stored tile stays until the data under it changes; and an admin can
  see and clear the cache. Subitems: PERF.130 (build the first levels
  ahead), PERF.131 (store and serve compressed), PERF.132 (proactive
  neighbours and next levels on a visit), PERF.133 (keep until the data
  changes), PERF.134 (admin: see and clear). It touches PERF.41 (the
  TILE_FORMAT stamp: a format change must drop the stored tiles once),
  MAP.239 (the tile root rises to the reach, which changes every level's
  geometry, so the build waits for it), MAP.195 (finer tiles leave out
  what a coarser tile sent, which changes what a tile holds), PERF.127
  (`planetgen warm`: the tile build is one of its families, each its own
  command, PERF.120), and the plan commands (a regenerated galaxy
  changes tile content, so the build is a step the wrapper lists after
  the generation commands, never a part of one). Owner: Core 2
  (proposed; the map and cache lane).
  Prerequisites: PERF.134.
  Related: PERF.41, PERF.104, PERF.120, PERF.127, MAP.158, MAP.159,
  MAP.195, MAP.239.
  Cut order (Boss, 2026-10-17, 6:48 PM EDT, MAP.250, Decided): the tiles
  stored here are built with halo and satellite-galaxy stars ranked
  below every other star, so a budget cut removes them first; landing
  that rule bumps the tile cache stamp and the cached tiles are rebuilt
  once. The galaxy map lag Boss reported at the same time is MAP.249; if
  its cause is the missing cache, this item is brought forward.
  Boss (2026-10-18, 5:43 PM EDT) widened this goal: the warm-up after
  every update, generation or change runs in phases and goes as deep as
  it can; the stored data may be about 10 times the 40 MB the first tile
  cache cost; the cache is capped at 1 GB by a setting (`cache.max_mb`,
  a slider on the settings page and a key in `config.json`); and every
  list of the site gets a cached index that regenerates when its data
  changes. Filed as PERF.139 (the setting), ADM.97 (the slider),
  PERF.141 (the phased warm-up) and, as one goal with the index and
  lists, DB.79, PERF.140 and UX.141 (issue #2293). Full wording on
  PERF.139.
  Contradiction sweep (Boss's request, 2026-10-18, 5:44 PM EDT; the
  newer note wins, report todo-contradictions-2026-10-18.md): "brought
  forward if its cause is the missing cache" is superseded by Boss's
  card on MAP.249 (2026-10-18, about 8:54 AM EDT, "Both, cut payload
  first"): the tile cache work follows MAP.249's payload cut.
  Decided (Boss, tapped "Skip it" on the card "Store Galaxy Map tiles
  compressed (PERF.131), or skip it?" at 11:27 AM EDT 2026-10-21, tap
  verified on the platform): PERF.131 is skipped and retired. Apache
  keeps compressing at send time (Core 2 measured under 0.1 s a big
  view: a 200-tile view is 3.8 MB packed and 0.8 MB gzipped, gzip 0.03
  to 0.10 s, against 3 to 54 s to build a cold view) and PERF.132
  (#2298) removed the real waits; no new wire format.

- [ ] **PERF.137 Audit the remaining `LIMIT ? OFFSET ?` queries: say which serve a big table and move those to keyset paging**
  Found by Core 5 (3:15 AM EDT 2026-10-18 as the lane reported), filed
  by the TODO thread. Keyset paging is done for the Systems, Uncharted
  stars and Phenomena tables (PERF.20 umbrella and PERF.75, #2154);
  `grep 'LIMIT ? OFFSET ?' src/planetgen` on main at 8.0.1795 still
  finds 16 sites, as candidates only (Core 5 did not trace which serve
  big tables): `db/query.py` lines 214, 501, 576, 618, 857, 898, 1781,
  2270, 2365, 4234 and 6045 (11 queries), `population/model.py` 695, 778
  and 830 (list queries), `db/stats.py` 310 (base names) and
  `queue/work.py` 907 (task listing). The API list routes take `offset`
  (api/routes.py MAX_PAGE_OFFSET) and `web/lib/pagination.py` clamps a
  page past the end. Why it matters: `OFFSET` makes page n cost n times
  as much (measured for the Systems table: rows 0, 20,000, 500,000 and
  1,500,000 take 0.004, 0.13, 5.8 and 12.1 s idle, where a keyset page
  costs 2 ms). Do: for each site, read the caller and the table it pages
  (row count at a full galaxy, from the schema or a measured count) and
  write one line per site: big or small, and the deepest page a user or
  the API can ask for. Move the big ones to the keyset form the three
  finished tables use (`after=<sort key, id>` next to `offset=`) and
  leave the small ones with a one-line comment saying the table stays
  under a few thousand rows. Done: a table of the 16 sites on this item
  with the verdict for each, every big site on keyset paging with a test
  that pages to the end, and the deepest-page time under 50 ms at a full
  galaxy. Owner: Core 5 (proposed, it found the list and wrote the
  PERF.126 and PERF.127 commands); low priority, no version blocker.
  Prerequisites: none. Related: PERF.75, PERF.135.

  Boss, 2026-10-18, 5:43 PM EDT: "I want multiple phases to our site

  generation or updates are done, anytime anything changes, the cache it
  belongs to gets automatically regenerated." And at 5:43 PM EDT: "Let's
  say I'm perfectly happy with the cache up to 1 GB. There should be a
  setting for that: how big the cache should be, on a slider on the
  settings page and also, of course, in the config JSON file." Do: build
  `object_index` per kind after generation and after `planetgen orbits`,
  and refresh a kind when its data version tag moves (the page cache
  already has per-kind tags in `web/lib/pagetags.py` and counters in
  `db/dataversion.py`, but nothing consumes a tag bump to rebuild): only
  the changed rows are rewritten, with a full rebuild as the fallback
  and a check that the index matches the live tables. The index counts
  against `cache.max_mb`. Done: after a generation run, an orbital
  update and an API edit each leave the index matching the live tables,
  a test changes one object and sees only its row rewritten, and the
  admin page shows the index size and age per kind. Suggested owner:
  Core 2; filed in 8.2.
  Decided (Boss, 2026-10-18, card taps 5:56 to 5:57 PM EDT, as the
  coordinator reported them): the index and lists are filed in 8.2 with

  reported 12:10 PM EDT 2026-10-21 as the lane reported; no epoch):
  `cache.max_mb` (default 1024, 0 turns the disk caches off, environment
  variable PLANETGEN_CACHE_MAX_MB) is the one budget; the stored lists
  and the index built here must share it and still need the "kept first"

- [ ] **PERF.144 Every job queued to RQ gets a time limit from the best available estimate of how long it takes, never no limit, so a killed worker's entry expires**
  Boss (2026-10-21, 12:44 PM EDT, in the Bug Hunt thread, as Bug Hunt
  reported it): "Can we build a time limit to assign to RQ based on
  stats?". Today the Generate page's job (`web/jobs.py:696`), the API's
  jobs (`queue/api_jobs.py:150`) and the queue executor
  (`queue/redisqueue.py:305`) are queued with `job_timeout=-1`, so RQ
  never expires their entries when a worker dies (PERF.142). Units
  already get a limit (`units.unit_timeout`: a multiple of the stage's
  expected seconds, with a floor and a ceiling, never -1).
  Do: audit every site that enqueues to RQ (the Generate page's job in
  `web/jobs.py`, the API's jobs in `queue/api_jobs.py`, the queue
  executor in `queue/redisqueue.py`, the units, and any other `enqueue`
  call, found by grep and listed on this item) and give each a finite
  `job_timeout` taken from the best estimate available, in this order:
  the recorded timings of that kind (`generation_stats`), the stage ETAs
  the run plan already computes, then the size of the work (sectors,
  systems, cells, span); the limit is a multiple of the estimate with a
  floor and a ceiling (as `units.unit_timeout` does), a fixed ceiling
  only for a route with no estimate at all, and never -1 or None. Boss,
  2026-10-21, 5:32 PM EDT (as the coordinator relayed): "I also want to
  make sure we've ensured that all jobs that go to RQ get a time limit
  based on how much time the system thinks it will take based on the
  best estimates avilable, so that RQ can help make sure we don't have
  dead jobs." Done: the audit list of enqueue sites is on this item;
  each site passes a finite limit; a test fails if any job is enqueued
  without a timeout (a guard on the one enqueue wrapper, or a grep-style
  test that fails on a bare `enqueue` call); a kind with recorded
  timings gets the multiple, one with only a size estimate gets the
  size-based limit, and one with neither gets the ceiling; and a job
  over its limit is ended and reported failed. Owner: Bug Hunt, first in
  its queue (priority raised by Boss, 5:32 PM EDT 2026-10-21; PERF.142
  and PERF.143 merged as #2345). Related: PERF.142, PERF.106 (the unit
  limits).
  Prerequisites: none. Related: PERF.142, PERF.143, PERF.106.

## DB: Database and schema

DB.1 shipped in 7.35.0 (PR #152). DB.2 to DB.5 done (PR #342, PR #347).

- [ ] **DB.9 Repair a damaged galaxy database from a parity file**
  Boss (same message): "then Phase 1 inject a DB repair using parity
  data stored in a file." Done:
  - Every sector gets a content checksum, the canonical hash of GEN.58's
    fingerprint.
  - A parity file kept outside the database (path in `config.json`)
    holds Reed-Solomon parity over groups of sector exports, so any one
    damaged sector per group can be rebuilt; the group size sets the
    overhead. It is updated whenever sectors are saved or edited, and
    carries its own checksum so damage to it is caught too.
  - `generate.py repair-db` uses DB.8's check to find damaged sectors
    and rebuilds each from the parity file. Where parity can't, and the
    galaxy's seed and version key match the running code (OPS.14), it
    regenerates the sector from its seed and replays its edits from the
    edit log. It re-runs the check and lists anything it could not
    repair.
  - A test damages rows in a copy of a small galaxy, repairs them, and
    gets a passing check.
  Research (2026-10-09, db-check-and-parity-repair.md): (1) replace "the
  canonical hash of GEN.58's fingerprint" with a separate storage
  checksum: SHA-256 over a lossless, id-preserving dump of the stored
  rows, read back after the write. (2) The checksum and the parity
  export omit the columns the daily orbit update rewrites (phases,
  positions, velocities, reflex offsets, binary positions, comet
  anomalies, and a placed object's `sector_id`; the list is in the
  design doc section 5.2). (3) Groups are built from sectors of similar
  export size, far apart in sector id, for an overhead of about 7
  percent. (4) The codec is an in-tree stdlib GF(256) Reed-Solomon
  module (`planetgen/util/rscodec.py`), no new dependency; default G =
  32, m = 2, both in `config.json`. (5) Add the delta update, the record
  format (per-record CRC, per-member checksums) and the stale-record
  decision table. (6) Repair rebuilds the table when a clustered-index
  page is unreadable (dump survivors with `innodb_force_recovery=1`,
  recreate, reload with FK checks off, insert rebuilt sectors with their
  ids). (7) The regenerate-from-seed fallback is split off as the new
  fallback item; this item needs DB.8 only. (8) The test flips bytes in
  an `.ibd` page of a copy while the server is stopped, not `UPDATE`s
  rows. (9) A `dirty` flag on the sector row, set by every writer of
  exported columns (`store.py` direct UPDATEs, `api/edits.py`,
  `db/edits.py`) and cleared after the parity update; listing those
  writers is part of the item. Before DB.19's mass cut `phenomenon_scatter`
  would be 1.17e9 rows and about 161 GB (the earlier 1.6e8 rows and 21 GB
  was an unverified estimate); after the cut it is about 2.7e5 rows.
  Decided (Boss, 2026-10-10 18:44Z, defaults approved; defaults taken):
  after a repair
  the orbit-updated columns come back as generated and the next orbit
  update carries on (a small daily snapshot of ids, phases and sector
  only if exact positions matter); G = 32, m = 2; repairing a bad
  clustered-index page may mean restarting the database server with
  `innodb_force_recovery=1`.
  Split (2026-10-16, Boss 1:07 PM EDT: look at each item for smaller
  chunks and shared work): this item is now the umbrella and is done
  when its subitems are: DB.43, DB.44, DB.45, DB.46, DB.47, DB.48. The
  largest item of the slice: a stdlib codec, a schema change, a checksum
  that every writer of exported columns must respect, a parity file kept
  current on every save, a repair command, and a table rebuild for an
  unreadable clustered-index page (nine research points in its text).
  Prerequisite GEN.57 dropped (2026-10-16 review): only the
  regenerate-from-seed fallback, DB.17, needs it; the parity half needs
  DB.8 only.
  Owner: Core 1 (Boss's lanes to 8.1, 2026-10-17, 10:06 AM EDT; lane
  assignment
  /mnt/project-files/reports/core1-5-lanes-to-8-1-2026-10-17.md). This replaces any earlier owner line on this item.
  Prerequisites: DB.43, DB.44, DB.45, DB.46, DB.47, DB.48.
  Design: [docs/design/reproducible-galaxies.md](design/reproducible-galaxies.md)

- [ ] **DB.29 update.sh and every database migration refuse to start while jobs are active, unless --yes is passed or the user confirms cancelling them**
  Boss, 2026-10-15 02:55Z: "Add TODO item, when migrating the database
  to a new version, if there are active jobs, ask the user to cancel the
  jobs first before changing anything." Widened by Boss, 02:56Z: "In
  fact, anytime update is run, it won't start without either --yes
  passed OR if the user specifically confirms they want to cancel all
  jobs prior to starting the upgrade or install." Done: before it
  changes anything, update.sh (every install and every upgrade, not only
  runs that migrate) and the migrate command check for active jobs
  (running or queued generation runs and other background jobs). With
  none, they proceed as before. With any, they list them and stop until
  either `--yes` was passed, or the user types an explicit confirmation
  that all active jobs may be cancelled; only then are the jobs
  cancelled, and then the install or upgrade starts. Boss, 02:59Z: "the
  update script needs to know if it's being run either from systemd or
  cron, and if it has, assume no unless --yes is passed. Or say 30
  seconds of waiting for input and it assumes no and cancels the
  update." So update.sh detects a run from systemd or cron (no person
  at the keyboard) and then assumes "no": it changes nothing and exits
  non-zero unless `--yes` was passed. When it does prompt, 30 seconds
  without an answer count as "no": it changes nothing and exits
  non-zero. Without `--yes` and without a terminal to ask on, it does
  the same.
  update.sh still never edits the user's Redis configuration (OPS.48).
  A test covers each path (no jobs, jobs and `--yes`, jobs and a typed
  confirmation, jobs and no answer within 30 seconds, jobs and a run
  from systemd or cron), and the check is the one place every
  migration goes through.
  Dependency: how the active jobs are read depends on the work queue
  steps. PERF.96 (run record and counters in Redis, done, PR #1553)
  supplies the library call that lists active runs, which the check
  uses; and PERF.99 supplies the cancel through the stop
  command, after which the check uses them. PERF.100 (which deletes the
  old work tables with a migration) must pass through this check too.
  Owner: Database, after DB.28 (done, PR #1476) and before PERF.100.
  Prerequisites: PERF.99. Related: PERF.95 (done, PR #1506), PERF.96
  (done, PR #1553), PERF.99, PERF.100, OPS.48, DB.18, DB.27 (done, PR

- [ ] **DB.33 MySQL 8.0.46 reflects the foreign keys fk_facilities_type and fk_facility_field_values_field as RESTRICT, so check-db calls a healthy database damaged (bug)**
  Reported by Quality (2026-10-15, 4:56 PM EDT run, relayed by the
  coordinator). On MySQL 8.0.46 the foreign keys `fk_facilities_type`
  and `fk_facility_field_values_field` reflect with `ondelete` RESTRICT
  while the models declare none, so `check-db` reports a healthy
  database as damaged and six tests fail (test_db_check, test_db_models,
  test_db_check_deep). Quality confirmed (2026-10-15, combined run) that
  it fails alone on a clean main, so no lane's change causes it; the six
  tests are test_a_healthy_database_passes,
  test_a_stale_system_count_is_a_warning_not_damage,
  test_the_command_exits_one_on_damage_and_zero_when_clean,
  test_models_match_a_database_built_from_schema_sql,
  test_a_changed_column_is_noticed and
  test_a_deep_check_off_a_terminal_needs_yes. Declaring
  ondelete='RESTRICT' alone would fix 8.0.46 but break MySQL 8.4 and
  MariaDB, which reflect none, so the compare must treat all three as
  equal. Fix: compare RESTRICT, NO ACTION and none as equal in
  `db/check.py` `_model_drift` and in `db/models.py`. Done: check-db
  passes on a healthy MySQL 8.0.46 database, the six tests pass, and a
  real drift in a foreign key's delete rule is still reported. Owner:
  Core (2026-10-15).
  Update (Core 1 and Core 2, 2026-10-15): the owner is now Core 2 (Core
  1 handed it over). Eight tests fail on MySQL 8.0.46, also

  information_schema column names come back upper case, the test reads

  they fail on main alone, always. Regenerating models.py with
  scripts/generate_db_models.py on that server makes the drift failures
  vanish, so the fix may also be a regenerate plus the case-insensitive
  read.
  Quality (2026-10-15, #1697): the test_db_check column-name case fix

- [ ] **DB.40 Parity data backup part: the parity file of the DB repair copied into the backup archive**
  Boss (2026-10-16, 1:59 PM and 2:00 PM EDT): "let's add backups of the
  control DB and backups of the parity data for DB repair." and "All
  those should be bz2 tarballed together." Boss (2:00 PM EDT): "we also
  have to build a way to use that data so build that out and let's make
  this targetted for v9.0 so incorporate the chain for these (restore /
  repair using backups) with that due date. Settings page is v8.1".
  Target 8.9 (the backups and repair chain, umbrella ADM.91); the
  settings page and the settings backups stay in 8.1 (ADM.83 to ADM.85).
  All backup pieces are parts of one `.tar.bz2` archive (ADM.87);
  retention is `settings.backups_kept` (default 20, 1 to 200). DB.9
  keeps parity for every sector in an append-only parity file outside
  the database (path in `config.json`). A damaged database is only
  repairable with a parity file that matches it, so the file is a backup
  part, written to `parity/`: the copy is taken under the parity
  writer's lock and cuts at the last complete record (the file is an
  append-only log of self-describing records with a header scan, so no
  index is stored); it can be switched off for a very large galaxy with
  the option `settings.backup_parity` (default on), and the manifest
  records its size and the sector count it covers. Done: the part
  registered with ADM.87, the lock-held copy under a concurrent save,
  and the size and coverage in the manifest (the restore is DB.41).
  Prerequisites: DB.46. Related: ADM.85, DB.8, DB.17.

- [ ] **DB.43 Reed-Solomon codec in the standard library: planetgen/util/rscodec.py**
  Split from DB.9 (2026-10-16, Boss 1:07 PM EDT: look at each item for
  smaller chunks and shared work). A GF(256) Reed-Solomon module with no
  new dependency: a Cauchy generator scaled so row 0 is plain XOR,
  `RS(k, m)` with `encode` (k equal-length blocks to m parity blocks),
  `decode` (any k of the k+m blocks back to the data) and `update` (new
  parity when one member changes, from the old and new bytes). The
  tested code is in docs/design/db-check-and-parity-repair.md 5.9. Why:
  the parity file (child d) and the repair command (child e) both stand
  on it, and it can be built and tested with no database. Done: the
  module and its tests: random erasure patterns of up to m blocks decode
  exactly for (k, m) of (16,1), (16,2), (32,2) and (8,3); `update`
  equals a fresh `encode`; unequal member lengths work through zero
  padding; the time to encode and to rebuild one 32-member group of 43
  KB blocks is recorded in the PR.
  Owner: Core 1 (Boss's lanes to 8.1, 2026-10-17, 10:06 AM EDT; lane
  assignment
  /mnt/project-files/reports/core1-5-lanes-to-8-1-2026-10-17.md). This replaces any earlier owner line on this item.

- [ ] **DB.45 Storage checksum and the dirty flag: the export, the checksum and every writer**
  Split from DB.9 (2026-10-16, Boss 1:07 PM EDT: look at each item for
  smaller chunks and shared work). Compute the sector's storage checksum
  as SHA-256 over a lossless, id-preserving dump of its stored rows,
  read back after the write, leaving out the columns the daily orbit
  update rewrites (phases, positions, velocities, reflex offsets, binary
  positions, comet anomalies, a placed object's `sector_id`; list in
  design section 5.2). Every writer of exported columns sets
  `parity_dirty` in its own transaction: the direct UPDATEs in
  `db/store.py` (names, positions, velocity), `api/edits.py` and
  `db/edits.py`; finding every writer is part of this item. DB.8's check
  reads the checksum and reports a dirty sector as "unprotected", not
  damaged. Why: the parity file can only be correct if a changed row is
  always noticed. Done: the export and checksum, every writer marked,
  and tests: each writer sets the flag; an orbit update does not change
  the checksum; a flipped stored value is reported as damage and a dirty
  sector as unprotected.
  Owner: Core 1 (Boss's lanes to 8.1, 2026-10-17, 10:06 AM EDT; lane
  assignment
  /mnt/project-files/reports/core1-5-lanes-to-8-1-2026-10-17.md). This replaces any earlier owner line on this item.
  Prerequisites: DB.44. Related: DB.9.

- [ ] **DB.46 The parity file: groups, records, a delta update on every save and the stale-record rule**
  Split from DB.9 (2026-10-16, Boss 1:07 PM EDT: look at each item for
  smaller chunks and shared work). A parity file kept outside the
  database (path in `config.json`) with G = 32 members and m = 2 parity
  blocks per group (both in `config.json`), groups formed at save time
  from sectors of one export-size class that are far apart in sector id
  (the W = 256 rule, shrinking for small galaxies); an append-only log
  of self-describing records (magic, format version, group id, `seq`,
  per-member address, length and checksum, parity bytes, CRC32C), an
  in-memory index rebuilt by a header scan, compaction as a function.
  Each save updates the group's parity from the member's before-image
  inside the saving transaction (`P_j' = P_j xor c_ji x (old xor new)`),
  after checking the before-image against its old checksum, then clears
  `parity_dirty`. The stale-record decision table of design 5.6 is code.
  Why: this is the part that makes repair possible and it must cost
  milliseconds per save. Done: the file, the update on save, and tests:
  save, edit and delete keep parity equal to a fresh encode; a torn tail
  loses nothing; a stale record is recomputed, not treated as damage;
  overhead is about 7 percent on a 1,000-sector fixture.
  Owner: Core 1 (Boss's lanes to 8.1, 2026-10-17, 10:06 AM EDT; lane
  assignment
  /mnt/project-files/reports/core1-5-lanes-to-8-1-2026-10-17.md). This replaces any earlier owner line on this item.
  Prerequisites: DB.43, DB.45. Related: DB.9.

- [ ] **DB.48 repair-db: rebuild the table when a clustered-index page is unreadable**
  Split from DB.9 (2026-10-16, Boss 1:07 PM EDT: look at each item for
  smaller chunks and shared work). When a page of the `sectors`
  clustered index cannot be read, rebuild the table: restart the
  database server with `innodb_force_recovery=1` (the command says so
  first and asks), dump the surviving rows, recreate the table, reload
  with foreign-key checks off, and insert the rebuilt sectors with their
  ids (design section 4). Why: single-sector rebuild in place does not
  work for a bad index page, and it is the one repair that needs a
  server restart, so it is a separate decision for the admin. Done: a

  stopped, runs the repair and gets a passing check with every sector

## API: The JSON API

- [ ] **API.3 Remote generate: generate on a local machine, upload through the API**
  Boss (2026-10-01 19:22Z): "using an API key add a remote-generate
  option where I can use generate.py with the right command lines to
  have my local system (much faster than the server-side) generate
  whatever I want and use the API to add it into the system once it's
  generated. Do not implement yet." Today `generate.py` writes straight
  to a MySQL/MariaDB database it can reach, and the API's write routes
  (`api/edits.py`, API.1's create-a-system route from PR #170) take one
  system or body at a time with an admin's API key. Done: `generate.py`
  gets a remote mode (for example `--remote URL --api-key KEY`) for the
  same commands and options as a local run (`sector`, `galaxy` modes,
  `plan`, the bright-star scatter and backfill, `population`); it asks
  the server for what it needs first (the galaxy's seed and skeleton,
  which sectors are already filled, the id and name state), generates
  on the local machine with all its workers, then uploads the results
  in batches to new API routes that check the key, validate each batch
  (ADM.5's validator), refuse sectors that were filled meanwhile, save
  them the same way a server-side run does (names, ids, bright-star
  levels, caches and tiles invalidated), and report what was added. A
  remote run appears in the job tree and job page (ADM.10, PR #294; ADM.12, PR #285) like
  a server-side one. Boss's answers (2026-10-01 19:28Z):
  - Generate and keep in memory: the local machine needs no database of
    its own.
  - The name indexes and id state are downloaded from the API once, for
    local use, so the run doesn't keep calling the API for them (the
    server reserves id blocks and claims the sectors for the run).
  - Uploads and downloads are compressed (gzip, bz2 or similar): some
    compression time is worth faster transfers.
  - Fully resumable: the local machine caches on disk every API call it
    means to send until the server confirms it; the server keeps a
    buffer of everything it receives, stages it, and writes to the
    database in a controlled way only complete units (a complete star
    system, a complete sector). This probably needs database changes
    so staged data can be stored and flagged incomplete until it is.
  - The local version must match the server's API version (API.4 and
    API.5).
  Boss's answers (2026-10-01 19:32Z):
  - Only an admin's API key can upload; user-level keys can read but
    never upload (API.6).
  - Upload limits are investigated and planned separately (API.7).
  - Reserved ids and claimed sectors stay reserved until the upload
    finishes or an admin clears it; nothing else may use them in the
    meantime. Admins see and clear incomplete uploads on their own page
    (ADM.13).
  - The server checks every upload and has the final say on what is
    written to the database (API.8).
  Order: API.4, API.5 and API.6 first (version and key scopes), then
  API.7's plan, then API.3's sub-items below with API.8 and ADM.13.
  Research (2026-10-09, api-design-standards.md): the upload unit is
  `StarSystem.to_dict()` objects in a versioned envelope, not table rows
  (rows named after `schema.sql` would force an API bump on nearly every
  migration). Measured 58.6 KB raw and 13.8 KB gzip per system.

  Prerequisites: API.30, ADM.95.

    admin clears it (ADM.13); server-side runs and other uploads skip
    claimed sectors.
    Research (2026-10-09, api-design-standards.md): reservation on the
    existing `_allocate_id` hi/lo mechanism, with a new

    When the claims exist, applying a change plan (ADM.60) refuses a

    Needs the upload bookkeeping tables (first child of API.11), which

- [ ] **API.4 API compatibility data in the docs**
  Boss (2026-10-01 19:28Z): "let's make API compatibility data and put
  that in the docs as another TODO item to add but not do yet." Done:
  the API has a version of its own, separate from the release number,
  and the docs carry a compatibility table: each API version, the
  release that introduced it, the routes and payload formats it
  changed, and which client versions (`generate.py` remote mode,
  API.3, and the web pages' `lib/apiclient.py`) can talk to which
  server versions. The table is updated in the same PR as any API
  change. Question (decided below): is the API version bumped by hand,
  or by a
  release note kind like `changes/<name>.api.md`?
  Research (2026-10-09, api-design-standards.md): answer the open
  question: the version is bumped by hand against a CI rule. A committed
  OpenAPI file for the remote contract (`docs/api/openapi.json`, built
  from the Pydantic models by `planetgen/api/spec.py`), `python -m
  planetgen.api.spec --check` in tests, and `oasdiff breaking` and
  `changelog` between PR base and head (a breaking diff means a higher
  MAJOR, any other diff a higher MINOR, none unchanged). No
  `changes/<name>.api.md` note kind. The compatibility contract covers
  the remote-client routes only. The table is generated from
  `planetgen/api/version.py` history, and the stamp job fills in the
  release number.
  Decided (2026-10-10): Boss (19:12Z): the API version is bumped by
  hand, with a CI check against the OpenAPI file.
  Owner: Core 2 (Boss's lanes to 8.1, 2026-10-17, 10:06 AM EDT; lane
  assignment
  /mnt/project-files/reports/core1-5-lanes-to-8-1-2026-10-17.md). This replaces any earlier owner line on this item.
  Prerequisites: API.26.

- [ ] **API.5 API version and compatibility checking**
  Boss (2026-10-01 19:28Z): "Another TODO item will be API version /
  compatibility checking so that we make sure the server knows how to
  take data from different client versions." Done: every API request
  carries the client's API version (a header); the server answers with
  its own version and the range it accepts (`/api/health`), refuses a
  client outside that range with a clear message saying which version
  to install, and, inside the range, reads older clients' payloads
  through converters so it knows how to take data from each supported
  version. `generate.py`'s remote mode (API.3) checks before it starts
  generating, not after. Built on API.4's compatibility data. Question
  (decided below): how many older versions the server keeps accepting.
  Research (2026-10-09, api-design-standards.md): answer "how many older
  versions": the current major, plus the previous major for one release
  cycle after a major bump, for upload payloads only (no read
  converters). Add `GET /api/version` (public, database-free, returns
  `api_version`, `min_client`, `max_client`, `release`, `version_key`,
  `galaxy_schema`) and the `PlanetGen-API-Version` header both ways;
  `generate.py --remote` checks before reading config. A refusal is `400
  api_version_unsupported` (or `410` past a sunset), not `426`; the
  check does not depend on `/api/health`. Add the version-key comparison
  (design doc 4.5). Decided (Boss, 2026-10-10 18:44Z, defaults approved;
  defaults taken): a remote
  client may differ in release within the accepted range, with a
  warning; a version-key mismatch (OS, architecture, Python) warns and
  does not refuse.
  Decided (2026-10-10): Boss (19:12Z): keep the current major plus the
  previous major for one release cycle (upload payloads only).
  Contradiction sweep (Boss's request, 2026-10-18, 5:44 PM EDT; the
  newer note wins, report todo-contradictions-2026-10-18.md): the
  version header is `X-PlanetGen-API-Version` (the code's
  `API_VERSION_HEADER`, docs/api.md, API.31 of 2026-10-17, 11:33 AM
  EDT), not `PlanetGen-API-Version`; and the server reports its version
  and accepted range at `GET /api/version` (2026-10-09 research), not
  only at `/api/health`, which may keep reporting `api_version`.

- [ ] **API.6 User-level API keys, owned by the account that created them, that can read but not upload**
  Boss (2026-10-01 19:32Z): "Only admin can upload, and Admin can
  create user-level API keys that can access but not upload." Today
  API keys (`admin_api_keys`) belong to admins and carry every admin
  right. Done: an admin can create, name, list and revoke user-level
  API keys; a user-level key can use the read routes (and anything
  later granted to users) but every write route, the remote upload
  routes of API.3 above all, answers 403 for it; an admin key keeps
  every right. Ties in with USR.1 and USR.2 (user accounts and roles)
  and PR #293 (TEST.44), which already answers 403 to
  any API key that makes keys, changes credentials or 2FA, or logs
  out. Decided (Boss, 2026-10-02 01:31Z): "all keys are attached to
  the account that created them". Every API key, admin or user-level,
  records the account that created it, and requests made with it act as
  that account. Today that is an admin account; once user accounts exist
  (USR.1, USR.2) a user's keys belong to that user, so this touches the
  user account work (USR): the key-to-account link for user accounts
  builds after USR.2. Logging every call is its own item, API.15,
  which doesn't wait for user accounts.
  Research (2026-10-09, settings-seo-and-accounts.md): effective rights
  are the intersection of the key's scope and the owner's current role,
  evaluated per request (open question for Boss, default: a user-level
  key made by an admin acts as the creating account with read-only
  scope).
  Prerequisites: DB.58, USR.26.

- [ ] **API.15 Log every API call with its user, how it came in, and its HTTP response code**
  Boss (2026-10-02 01:31Z): "all api call logs should log the user that
  called for it and if it was called through an api key or someone
  logged into the web site or from the console (console user will just
  be called god). Standard will have all API calls logged and what
  response they generated back (use HTTP responses codes and note in
  documentation that you're using HTTP response codes for parity with
  web logs)." Done: by default every API call is logged with the time,
  the route, the account that made it (the key's owner for an API key,
  the signed-in user for the web site, and "god" for the console), how
  it came in (API key, web session or console), and the HTTP response
  code it got back; the API docs say that HTTP response codes are used
  for parity with the web server's logs; a test makes a call each way
  and checks the log rows. Needs no user accounts: it logs today's admin
  accounts (and "god"), so it is placed in phase 0, ahead of API.6; once
  user accounts exist (USR.1) the logged user can be any account.
  Research (2026-10-09, api-design-standards.md): log through the
  activity log first (a new `API` category in `CATEGORIES` and
  `docs/config.md`), with `X-Request-Id`, an `after_request` hook,
  `internal=1` for in-process page calls (about 6 per page view) and an
  `api_log.internal` setting, and the privacy and retention paragraph
  (open question for Boss, default 30 days full IP, then truncated, 13
  months total). An `api_calls` table with a background writer only when
  an admin page needs queries. "Console" in `god` means API-shaped
  actions run by CLI tools without a request; existing `GEN` lines
  unchanged.
  Owner: Core 2 (Boss's lanes to 8.1, 2026-10-17, 10:06 AM EDT; lane
  assignment
  /mnt/project-files/reports/core1-5-lanes-to-8-1-2026-10-17.md). This replaces any earlier owner line on this item.

  Boss (2026-10-01 19:32Z): "the API will have to have a reliable method
  of syncing and making sure uploaded data is verified good before it
  is finalized in the DB, the server has the final say in how items are
  added to the database." Done: the client and server agree, by batch
  and by unit (a star system, a sector), on what has been sent and
  received, with checksums, so nothing is lost or written twice; every
  staged unit is checked on the server before it is finalized
  (complete, well formed, inside its reserved sector and id block,
  names unique, and the physics checks of ADM.5's validator); the
  server finalizes a unit in one transaction or rejects it with the
  reasons, and may correct what it can (renaming a clashing name,
  re-running derived values) rather than trusting the client's copy.
  Question (decided below): which corrections the server makes on its
  own, and
  which reject the unit so the client regenerates it.
  Research (2026-10-09, api-design-standards.md): adopt the auto-correct
  versus reject rule (design doc 7.4) as the default answer: correct
  only a clashing name and pure derived columns; reject everything else;
  the server returns a rename map; a rejection does not release the
  claim.
  Decided (2026-10-10): Boss (19:16Z, Accept all): the server auto-fixes
  only a clashing name and purely derived columns, and rejects
  everything else so the client regenerates it.
  Narrowed (2026-10-16, Boss 1:33 PM EDT): the checks, the
  one-transaction finalize and the limited auto-fix are the unit
  finalizer ADM.82, built in 8.6 for change plans. This item is what
  remains: the batch and unit sync with checksums, the staged units, and
  calling the finalizer when a unit is sealed.
  Prerequisites: ADM.82.

  existing API version header (`API_VERSION_HEADER`,
  `X-PlanetGen-API-Version`) with the same API version instead, and the
  server keeps logging both (API.15). Done: one function builds the user

  choose to have the computer put the new star system in the least

- [ ] **ADM.58 Change plan engine: operations, the effect diff and the plan states, as a library**
  Boss (2026-10-16, 1:07 PM EDT), headline of 8.6 (ADM.57): the admin
  has complete control; the world adjusts to what the admin wants, after
  the admin approves the generation plan. A plan is an ordered list of
  operations (move an object, set an aspect, regenerate with a keep set,
  add, remove) on stored objects. Build `planetgen/admin/plans.py`: the
  operation types, validation of each against the stored object (Hill
  spheres, spacing, bounds), the computed effect diff (every row that
  would change, with before and after, and every object touched
  indirectly), the state machine (draft, requested, proposed, approved,
  applied, undone, stale, rejected, withdrawn: `requested` is a plan
  someone below the approving role submitted, used by 10.0 and built
  here so no state is added later; an admin's own plan goes from draft
  to proposed and the same admin confirms it, with no second approver,
  Boss 2026-10-16, 1:49 PM EDT; every transition records who and in
  which role) and the stale check (a plan is stale when any
  object it touches changed after the plan was proposed). An operation
  serialises in the versioned envelope the remote upload uses
  (`StarSystem.to_dict()`, API.13), so a plan and an upload describe a
  system the same way. Pure Python over loaded objects, no database, so
  it can be tested on its own. Done: the library with unit tests for
  every operation kind, the diff and the stale check.
  Staleness (2026-10-16 review): "changed" means changed by an edit (the
  journal row or an edit-version stamp per object), not by the nightly
  orbital update; a pending move or orbit plan re-bases its before
  values after an update has run and the approval screen shows the
  drift. Add "orbital update movement" to the tests.
  Waits for 8.6 (Boss, 2026-10-16, 3:00 PM EDT: a global top blocker
  that is not started before its version); no lane yet.
  Prerequisites: none. Related: ADM.57, ADM.6, ADM.7, ADM.8.
  Design: [docs/design/edit-everything.md](design/edit-everything.md)

- [ ] **ADM.94 Density override store and the fill read: set, undo and combine overrides for any region, and have later fills use them**
  Split from MAP.119 (2026-10-16, Boss 1:07 PM EDT: look at each item
  for smaller chunks and shared work). Write the library under
  planetgen/admin: `set_override(region, multiplier, admin, reason)`,
  `undo_override(id)` (append-only, the undo is a reverse row),
  `multiplier_for(sector)` combining overlapping regions in a stated
  order (narrowest wins), the range 0.1 to 10 on a log scale (a typed
  value beyond it with a warning), an activity-log entry for each
  change, and the read in the sector fill so a later fill multiplies its
  `--density` and records `density_multiplier_used` and `override_id`.
  Only unfilled sectors are affected; the function reports how many
  sectors in a region are filled and unaffected. A block or slab is a
  region object (GEN.302), so there is no separate block-or-slab path.
  Done: the library over `region_density_overrides` (DB.38), the fill
  read, and tests for set, undo, two overlapping regions in a stated
  order, a filled sector left alone and the logged entry.
  Prerequisites: DB.38, DB.60, GEN.302. Related: MAP.119.

- [ ] **ADM.97 The settings page can show a number as a slider: the cache size is the first one**
  Boss, 2026-10-18, 5:43 PM EDT: "I want multiple phases to our site

  where we rebuild our tile cache, and I want us to go as deep as we
  can. Last time the tile cache only cost like 40 MB. I'm okay with 10
  times that amount of stored data. If we can precalculate it, prepare
  it, and get it ready to ship, let's do it. Same thing for caches of
  all the lists. I had a serious problem with trying to find objects. I
  need an index. I need a list of systems. I need a list of basically
  every list the site wants, from phenomena in each type to planets to
  moons to stars to whatever. We should build a cached index. Once
  generation or updates are done, anytime anything changes, the cache it
  belongs to gets automatically regenerated." And at 5:43 PM EDT: "Let's
  say I'm perfectly happy with the cache up to 1 GB. There should be a
  setting for that: how big the cache should be, on a slider on the

  moving it writes the key, editing `config.json` moves the slider, and

  Merged with PERF.139 and PERF.133 (Core 2, #2316, release 8.0.1853,

  reason unless the admin chose otherwise. Done: a second submit while a

  without its confirmation is refused. Owner: the admin redesign thread

  Settings first, then the shell and palette, then Generate).
